title: How do you solve polynomial equations over Q? A museum tour
intro: **A self-guided “museum tour” for math**, after Bianca Viray's talk. Press **→** for the tour; the code runs live in your browser.

nodes.title: How do you solve polynomial equations?
nodes.text: Over $\mathbb{Q}$: find the **rational** solutions of $f(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = 0$, with $f$ having rational coefficients.

children.title: Rational roots
children.text: A rational root $p/q$ in lowest terms has $p \mid a_0$ and $q \mid a_n$: finitely many to try. Better: factor over $\mathbb{Q}$.

children.title: ...and the others?
children.text: Galois: the roots can be written with radicals exactly when the Galois group is solvable. $x^5 - x - 1$ has group $S_5$ (5T5): no formula.

children.title: Degree 2: conics
children.text: Hasse–Minkowski: a conic has a rational point iff it has one over $\mathbb{R}$ and over every $\mathbb{Q}_p$. Then the lines through one point give them all:
children.code:
t = var('t')
X, Y = (1 - t^2)/(1 + t^2), 2*t/(1 + t^2)   # on x^2 + y^2 = 1
pts = [(X(t=s), Y(t=s)) for s in [1/2, 2/3, 3/7]]
print(pts)
print([a^2 + b^2 for a, b in pts])

children.title: Degree 3: elliptic curves
children.text: Mordell: the rational points form a finitely generated group. $y^2 = x^3 - 2x$ has rank 1: chords and tangents from one point give infinitely many.
children.code:
E = EllipticCurve([0, 0, 0, -2, 0])
print('rank', E.rank(), 'generator', E.gens())
P = E.gens()[0]
for n in [2, 3]:
    print(n, '*P =', n*P)

children.title: Higher genus
children.text: Faltings: a curve of genus $\ge 2$ has only **finitely many** rational points. A search for small ones on $y^2 = x^5 - x + 1$ (each with $\pm y$):

nodes.title: Everything together!
nodes.text: Is there an **algorithm** that decides whether any polynomial equation has a rational solution? Over $\mathbb{Z}$ there is none (Hilbert's 10th problem: Matiyasevich, 1970). Over $\mathbb{Q}$ the question was long open; a proof that it is undecidable too was claimed in September 2026 (an OpenAI preprint, not yet formalized or refereed). For surfaces the local–global principle can fail (the Brauer–Manin obstruction).

steps.say: A museum tour: **→** moves on. Each box with code runs live in your browser (Sage), and you can change it: **Edit**, double-click a box, Shift+Enter.
One variable, rational roots: finitely many candidates, and factoring over $\mathbb{Q}$ finds them.
The other roots: is there a formula? Only if the Galois group is solvable. $S_5$ is not.
Two variables, degree 2: the local–global principle holds, and one point gives them all.
Degree 3: a finitely generated group of points. Try another curve: change the coefficients.
Genus 2 and up: finitely many points (Faltings), but finding them all is hard.
Everything together: no algorithm over $\mathbb{Z}$; over $\mathbb{Q}$, a claimed proof (2026) awaits checking.
